summary: Specifies Mobile IP for IPv4, which lets a mobile node keep its home address while moving between networks. A home agent forwards traffic to the node's current location. It replaces RFC 3220 and was itself replaced by RFC 5944.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IPv4 lets a device keep its home IP address when it connects through another network. A home agent forwards packets for that address to the device's current location.

subtitle: How an IPv4 device keeps its home address while attached to another network.

tldr.problem: IPv4 routing expects a device to receive packets on the network identified by its address. Moving can break connections, while advertising a separate route for every moving device does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A mobile node registers a care-of address with its home agent. The home agent intercepts packets for the home address and tunnels them to the node's current point of attachment.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3344 obsoleted RFC 3220 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 5944. RFC 4636 and RFC 4721 updated it.

today: RFC 3344, a Proposed Standard, obsoleted RFC 3220 and has been obsoleted by RFC 5944. It was updated by RFC 4636 and RFC 4721.

sections.title: The Mobility Problem
sections.content:
In IPv4, an address identifies a node's point of attachment. If the node changes networks, it can change addresses and lose existing connections, or require host-specific routes to spread through much of the Internet.

Mobile IP is designed for movement between IP subnets while keeping the node's address unchanged. It assumes movement is not generally more frequent than once per second and distinguishes this broader mobility from faster movement within one subnet.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv4 address normally identifies where a device connects. Mobile IP lets the device move between subnets without changing that address.

sections.title: Agents and Care-of Addresses
sections.content:
A mobile node has a long-term home address. When it is away, it also uses a care-of address that marks the end of a tunnel to its current location. A home agent on the home network keeps the location binding and tunnels packets to that address.

A foreign agent on the visited network can provide a care-of address and remove the tunnel wrapper. Alternatively, the mobile node can obtain its own local care-of address and remove the wrapper itself. In the return direction, ordinary IP routing generally carries the node's packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The home address stays with the device. A care-of address tells the home agent where to send packets while the device is away.

sections.title: Discovery and Registration
sections.content:
Mobile nodes use Agent Discovery to learn whether a network is home or foreign and to find mobility agents. Mobile IP extends ICMP Router Discovery: agents advertise their services, and a node can solicit an advertisement.

A node away from home sends a Registration Request with its home address, home agent, care-of address, lifetime and identification value. The home agent replies with acceptance or denial. Registration messages use UDP port 434, and a home-agent reply and every request require an authentication extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Agents announce their services on a network. The mobile device registers its current care-of address with its home agent, which confirms or rejects the request.

sections.title: Forwarding Packets Through a Tunnel
sections.content:
The home agent intercepts packets addressed to the mobile node's home address and encapsulates them for delivery to the care-of address. The tunnel ends at a foreign agent or at the mobile node, depending on which kind of care-of address is registered.

Home and foreign agents must support IP-in-IP encapsulation. The RFC also specifies how agents handle routing, broadcasts, multicast traffic and address resolution, and discusses reverse tunneling where ordinary routing may reject a packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The home agent wraps a packet in another IP packet and sends it to the care-of address. At the tunnel endpoint, the wrapper is removed and the original packet is delivered.

sections.title: Authentication and Replay Protection
sections.content:
Registration changes where a mobile node's traffic goes, so the RFC requires authentication to prevent a remote party from redirecting it. The default authentication algorithm is HMAC-MD5 with a 128-bit key.

A 64-bit Identification value helps match requests to replies and protect against replaying old registrations. The RFC also notes that Agent Advertisements and ARP are not authenticated by this protocol and discusses the risks of forged information on a local link.
sections.plainLanguage: A registration must prove that it came from an authorized party. The identification value also helps reject an old request sent again later.
